title: A New Relaxation for Tree-Based Problems and Minimum Power-Cost Spanning Trees
abstract: In this paper, we investigate lower bounds of tree-based optimization problems in order to obtain effective exact algorithms, such as branch-and-bound algorithms. Our new approach inherits the development of dynamic programming algorithms for constrained shortest path problems, as they occur as subproblems in Lagrangian relaxation algorithms and column generation-based algorithms for variants of the Vehicle Routing Problem. In the q-route relaxation, paths must satisfy a capacity constraint while the elementarity constraint is relaxed, that is, paths may contain cycles. An analogue of q-routes for tree optimization problems are q-arbs, a structure that relaxes elementarity for arborescences. We introduce a generalized formulation of q-arbs for a broad class of tree-based problems, and apply the neighborhood restrictions of so-called ng-routes to them to obtain tighter bounds. We apply the new dynamic programming approach to the Minimum Power-Cost Spanning Tree Problem and show empirically that the resulting bounds are often better than traditional LP-based lower bounds of (mixed) integer programming models.

 1      Introduction

For many classical NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, lower bounds (assuming
minimization) on the objective function value obtained by the linear relaxation of an integer
programming formulation are often of high quality, leading to very efficient algorithms, for
example when used within branch-and-bound. However, for well-solvable problems such as
the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and the Minimum Spanning Tree problem (MST),
it can be observed that the addition of side constraints (such as time-window constraints for
the TSP or hop constraints for the MST) often makes these problems much more difficult
to solve. One reason for this is that the lower bounds provided by the linear relaxations
of corresponding (extended) formulations tend to be weaker. With weak bounds only, a
branch-and-bound approach may then be restricted to small instances or instances with tight
constraints. Hence, other methods to compute lower bounds have been developed. In this
paper, we consider dynamic programming algorithms applied to state-space relaxations of
tree optimization problems.

           As a main example, we will use the Minimum Power Cost Spanning Tree problem
       (MPCST), also referred to as the All-to-All Broadcast, Power Range Assignment, or Symmetric
       Connectivity problem. The MPCST is an NP-hard variant of the MST, and it has been studied
       in several contexts (we will define it formally in Section 6). Notably, general incremental
       algorithms fail to guarantee optimal solutions for the MPCST [12]. Therefore, existing exact
       algorithmic approaches are largely based on mixed-integer programming [1, 8, 10]. We will
       present a novel dynamic programming formulation for the MPCST.
           Our new approach inherits the historical development of dynamic programming algorithms
       for constrained shortest path problems, as they arise as sub-problems in Lagrangian relaxation
       algorithms and column generation-based algorithms for variants of the Vehicle Routing
       problem (VRP). In the q-route relaxation, paths must fulfill a capacity constraint while
       the elementarity constraint is relaxed, i.e., paths may contain cycles. Similarly, the t-route
       relaxation allows only time-window feasible paths, but relaxes the elementarity condition, too.
       These relaxations lead to practically solvable sub-problems that are otherwise too difficult,
       since they have to be solved several times with varying (reduced) costs. The consequence
       of allowing non-elementary paths comes at the cost of a generally weaker bound in the
       Lagrangian relaxation or branch-and-price algorithm. Therefore, stronger relaxations were
       developed such as those that eliminate all 2-cycles [6] or all cycles of length ≤ k for a given
       constant k [7], and the ng-route relaxation [2]. The latter clearly constitutes the state of the
       art in branch-price-and-cut (BPC) algorithms for variants of the VRP [4].
           An analogue of q-routes for tree optimization problems are q-arbs, a structure that relaxes
       elementarity for arborescences. It was proposed by Uchoa et al. [11] for solving the otherwise
       prohibitively difficult pricing subproblems in a BPC algorithm to the Capacitated Minimum
       Spanning Tree problem (CMST). To our knowledge, the q-arb relaxation has neither been
       applied to any other tree optimization problem, nor has it been developed into a stronger
       relaxation in order to provide tighter lower bounds. We will define the ng-arb relaxation,
       which is stronger than the q-arb relaxation, and show that it is applicable to a broad class of
       tree optimization problems.
           For what follows, it is important to stress that dynamic programming is a method that
       works with equivalence classes of partial solutions. For example, in an unconstrained shortest
       path problem where s-to-t paths need to be computed, a partial path P = (s, . . . , i) from s
       to some vertex i lies in the equivalence class [P ] of all paths that start in s and end in i
       (examples of corresponding algorithms are the well-known algorithms of Dijkstra or Bellman
       and Ford). Therefore, the equivalence class of these paths can be described uniquely by i, and
       a cost-label c(i) is attached to each equivalence class. The dynamic programming algorithm
       initializes the labels (to 0 or ∞) and computes and possibly updates them in the course of
       the algorithm. Such an update happens when a partial path is extended along an arc (i, j)
       so that a new path P = (s, . . . , i, j) results. Some constrained problems may require a more
       fine-grained definition of equivalence classes and herewith more elaborate labels (e.g., the
       above ng-route relaxation uses labels c(i, S) for all paths that end at i and have an associated
       set S of vertices which are visited and “not forgotten”, see Section 4). In Section 5, we define
       the formal requirement on those equivalence classes and derive classes for arborescences that
       meet those. In Section 6, we discuss different equivalence classes for the MPCST.
           The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Basic definitions are provided
       in Section 2. Section 3 presents the recursive construction of an arborescence, as first
       suggested by Uchoa et al. [11], which allows us to define extensions of arborescences. For
       tree optimization problems, we introduce a new relaxation in Section 4 that we denote
       as ng-arb; it resembles the idea of the ng-route relaxation for constrained shortest path

 2      Basic Definitions
Let a digraph G = (V, A, c) be given, with vertices V and arcs A ⊆ V × V . For convenience,
we assume V = {1, . . . , n} and that G is simple, i.e., A does not include parallel arcs or
loops. For V ′ ⊂ V , G′ = (V ′ , A[V ′ ]) is the induced subgraph on V ′ , with A[V ′ ] := {(u, v) ∈
A | u, v ∈ V ′ }.
    A path P = (v0 , ..., vk ) in G is a sequence of vertices with (vi−1 , vi ) ∈ A for all 1 ≤ i ≤ k.
An undirected path allows (vi−1 , vi ) ∈ A or (vi , vi−1 ) ∈ A (or both) for all 1 ≤ i ≤ k. We say
that the path starts in v0 , ends in vk , and has length k. The path P = (v0 ) has length 0. If all
vertices in P are distinct, the path is elementary. Otherwise, if vi = vj for some 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k,
the path contains the cycle (vi , . . . , vj ). For an undirected path P = (v0 , . . . , vk ), the reversed
sequence of vertices is denoted by P̄ = (vk , . . . , v0 ). Since P̄ is an undirected path again, it
can be denoted as the reversed path to P .
    In the following, we want to allow that an arborescence contains an arc or a vertex
more than once. Hence, we assume that each arborescence has its own copy of a vertex.
These copies are called nodes for a clear distinction. We do not use different terms for arcs,
but we ensure that, for each arc between two nodes in an arborescence T , the arc between
the corresponding vertices exists in G. Hence, we can use sets VT and AT ⊆ VT × VT to
describe the nodes (copies of the vertices) and arcs (between nodes) which are contained in
the arborescence.

also [2]).

        5      Dynamic Programming
       Notice that arborescences and ng-arborescences are supersets of trees and hence optimizing
       over all arborescences gives lower bounds for tree problems. A tree problem is given by
       a subset Π′ of trees called the feasible trees and a cost-function assigning a cost to each
       (feasible) tree. To use the approach, we assume that the set of trees can naturally enlarged to
       a set Π of arborescences, i.e. Π′ ⊆ Π and an extension to the cost function to arborescences.
       Consider for example the degree constrained spanning tree problem. As the cost of a tree
       is just the sum of the costs of its edges, the same definition can be used for arborescences
       (counting edges multiple times if they appear several times in the arborescence). The set Π
       can be defined as the set of arborescences where the degree of each copy of a node is bounded
       (and hence, the degree of the corresponding vertices can be larger).

 6     The Minimum Power Cost Spanning Tree Problem
For an undirected weighted graph G = (V, E, c), the power cost of a spanning tree T = (V, ET )
is the sum of the cost of the maximum-cost edges incident to each vertex. The MPCST aims
to find a spanning tree with minimum power cost. An equivalent formulation is the all-to-all
broadcast problem or the symmetric connectivity problem, which assign transmission ranges
to vertices, and establish a connected network through all edges lying within the transmission
ranges of both incident vertices. For a minimum power cost spanning tree T ∗ , there is a
minimum cost range assignment whose established network contains T ∗ , and vice versa.
This makes the formulations equivalent. The MPCST problem is usually considered on
complete graphs with edge costs c(v, w) = ∥vw∥κ2 , where ∥·∥2 is the Euclidean distance
between vertices (given by points in the Euclidean plane), and κ is a coefficient usually
between 2 and 4 [1, 8, 10]. We consider G′ = (V, A, c′ ), the corresponding weighted digraph
to G as noted in Section 5. For an arborescence T ′ on G′ , we define its power cost as the sum
of maximum-cost arcs incident to each vertex, no matter their direction. Then a minimum
power cost spanning tree on G is equivalent to a minimum power cost spanning arborescence
on G′ .

 8     Conclusion

We have proposed a general q-arb dynamic programming formulation analogous to q-routes
known from VRP subproblems in Lagrangian relaxation and column generation. The proposed
formulation is not restricted to a specific tree optimization problem and allows for different
types of relaxation. In addition, we have introduced a new ng-relaxation for arborescences,
including a technique to compose efficient dynamic programs through equivalence classes.
    For the MPCST, we have described the first incremental recursive formulation that
provides optimal solutions, enabling us to apply a dynamic programming approach to this
problem. We have applied the ng-arb formulation to the MPCST and given an algorithm to
compute a lower bound in polynomial time. Computational results obtained on standard
MPCST instanced have shown that lower bounds obtained with the ng-arb formulation
compare favorably against the currently leading LP-based bounds.
    Our bounds may further be improved by applying additional relaxation-strengthening
methods such as adaptive neighborhood extension, discouraging cycles through Lagrangian
penalties, etc. Moreover, our current implementation does not use any type of dominance to
eliminate redundant intermediate solutions as of yet, and doing so may further reduce the
actual size of the dynamic programming table.
